claims.text: Reliable formation of noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles is governed by thermodynamically driven surface segregation.
Enhanced catalytic performance is governed by thermodynamically driven surface segregation.
Surface segregation produces a noble metal–rich shell over a multicomponent core.
The noble metal–rich shell creates catalytic sites with modified electronic properties.
The modified electronic properties optimize adsorption energies for reaction intermediates.
As-synthesized HEA nanoparticles containing noble and transition metals have a uniform, random elemental distribution.
Controlled post-synthesis thermal annealing or reductive treatment promotes surface segregation relative to rapid quenching.
The resulting noble metal–enriched surface is structurally and electronically different from the alloyed core.
Differences in surface free energies drive noble metal atoms to segregate to the nanoparticle surface during annealing.
Noble metal surface enrichment alters the local surface bonding environment.
Noble metal surface enrichment alters the surface strain state.
Changes in local bonding and strain modulate adsorption energies.
Changes in local bonding and strain alter catalytic reaction pathways.
The core–shell architecture stabilizes active catalytic sites.
The core–shell architecture improves catalytic selectivity.
The core–shell architecture increases turnover frequency.
Annealed HEA nanoparticles will show greater noble metal surface enrichment than rapidly quenched controls.
Annealed HEA nanoparticles will exhibit higher catalytic activity and selectivity than uniformly alloyed controls in reactions such as CO oxidation or oxygen reduction.
The proposed behavior should hold for approximately 5–10 nm HEA nanoparticles annealed in mild reducing atmospheres at temperatures up to about 300 °C.
The proposed behavior may not apply to larger particles, oxidizing conditions, or protocols that cause immediate phase separation.
